If it is a straight line on a log scale: the slope is "the change on the Y axis when the X value becomes 10 times larger". For diluting a strong acid, check whether pH rises by about 1 each time.

Curve fit: the closer R² is to 1, the better the fit. ‘Auto’ picks the best-fitting equation, but chooses a more complex one only if R² is clearly better. Always also consider whether the equation fits the principle of the experiment.
Tangent: the rate of change at that instant ({u}).
Compare the slopes early and late in the reaction to see how the reaction rate changes.
Area: the area between the curve and the X axis ({u}). To calculate only a selected range, drag on the graph.
Rate graph: where the value changes fastest shows up as a peak. In a titration, the peak position is the equivalence point.
Equivalence point: where pH changes most sharply. Use this volume to calculate the molar concentration of the sample. For a weak acid, the pH at the half-equivalence point equals pKa.
Plateau: the longest stretch where the value barely changes. On a cooling curve, this temperature is the freezing point.
Drag on the graph to select a range and calculate its mean and change. Try analyzing with Curve fit, Tangent and Area.
